name: Malian Tigadèguèna
description: Tigadèguèna, meaning 'peanut paste sauce' in Bambara, genuinely originated with the Mandinka and Bambara people of Mali before spreading across the region - real Malian versions are traditionally thinner and more watery than Senegalese maafe, and traditionally include real unrefined shea butter alongside the peanut paste, which isn't a distinct item here, so this version leans on peanut butter alone, missing shea butter's real earthy richness. Real Malian tigadèguèna is traditionally served with tô or fonio rather than rice.
steps_detailed: Brown the chicken with the onion, garlic, and ginger, 8-9 minutes.
Whisk the peanut butter with the tomatoes and 1.5 cups water, keeping it on the thinner, more watery side rather than a thick paste, and add to the pot.
Add the carrot and simmer 25-28 minutes until the chicken is tender.

name: Malian Tô
description: Tô, a stiff millet or sorghum porridge, is Mali's most essential staple starch, traditionally served with tigadèguèna and other sauces - real millet or sorghum flour isn't a distinct item here, so cornmeal stands in for a similarly stiff, cohesive texture.

ingredients.note: standing in for millet or sorghum flour

steps_detailed: Whisk about a third of the cornmeal with the salt into 1.25 cups boiling water.
Gradually beat in the remaining cornmeal, stirring vigorously, over medium-low heat 15-18 minutes, until very thick and it pulls away from the sides of the pot.

name: Malian Riz au Gras
description: Riz au gras, meaning 'fat rice', a rich tomato-and-meat rice dish, is a common Malian one-pot meal shared across the wider Francophone West African region.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef with the onion, 6-7 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and carrot, and simmer 10 minutes.
Stir in the rice and 1.25 cups water, cover, and simmer 18-20 minutes until tender.

name: Malian Fonio
description: Fonio, an ancient West African grain genuinely native to the Sahel region including Mali, is prized for cooking quickly and having a light, couscous-like texture - fonio isn't a distinct item here, so couscous stands in for a similarly light, quick-cooking grain.
steps_detailed: Bring water to a boil with the salt, pour over the couscous, cover, and let steam 5 minutes.
Fluff with a fork before serving.
steps: Bring water to a boil with the salt, pour over the couscous, cover, and let steam 5 minutes.

name: Malian Poulet Yassa
description: Poulet yassa, chicken marinated and slow-cooked in caramelized onions and lemon, shared with neighboring Senegal, real technique cooking the onions down until genuinely sweet, not just softened.
steps_detailed: Marinate the chicken in the lemon juice and garlic for at least 20 minutes.
Brown the chicken in a little oil, 6-7 minutes, then set aside.
Cook the onion over medium-low heat, stirring often, 20-25 minutes, until deeply softened and sweet.
Return the chicken with a splash of water and simmer 15 minutes more.

name: Malian Bouillie
description: Bouillie, a smooth millet porridge sweetened with sugar, a beloved Malian breakfast - real millet flour isn't a distinct item here, so cornmeal stands in for a similarly smooth, grain-based porridge.
steps_detailed: Whisk the cornmeal into 1 cup boiling water and cook, stirring, 10-12 minutes until smooth.
Stir in the milk and sugar.

name: Malian Grilled Fish
description: Grilled fish rubbed with garlic and pepper, reflecting Mali's Niger River fishing tradition.
steps_detailed: Rub the fish with the garlic and jalapeño, and let sit 10 minutes.
Grill or broil, 4-5 minutes per side, until just cooked through.

name: Malian Beignets
description: Beignets, sweet fried dough balls, a beloved Malian breakfast snack shared across much of West Africa.
steps_detailed: Whisk the flour, sugar, and baking powder with water into a thick batter.
Drop spoonfuls into hot oil and fry, turning, 4-5 minutes, until deeply golden.

name: Malian Fakoye
description: Fakoye is genuinely built on real jute (molokhia) leaves, dried and ground into a powder, which give the sauce its distinctive dark color and silky, slightly mucilaginous texture, closer in character to okra than to a simple leafy green stew - this is a very different dish from what was built here before, which was essentially plain spinach and beef. Real versions also lean on real dried fish and lamb, and a Songhai spice blend that isn't a distinct item here; okra stands in for jute's real texture, and spinach for the leaf, though this honestly misses the dish's real dark color and distinctive mucilage.

standing in for ground jute leaf

steps_detailed: Brown the lamb with the onion and jalapeño, 6-7 minutes.
Add the cumin and 1.5 cups water, and simmer 10 minutes.
Add the okra and simmer 10-12 minutes until it releases its real mucilage and the sauce turns notably silky.
Add the spinach and simmer 8-10 minutes more until wilted and the sauce has thickened and darkened.

name: Malian Mint Tea
description: Attaya, sweet mint tea poured with real ceremony, is central to Malian and wider West African hospitality.
steps_detailed: Warm the tea with the mint 5 minutes.
Stir in the sugar until dissolved.
Pour from a height into small glasses to build a light foam, a genuine part of how it's traditionally served.
